stem: Which approach to HRM treats employees mainly as a **resource to be used efficiently** and a cost to be controlled?

options.content: Hard HRM
options.rationale: Correct: the focus is on control, targets and keeping labour cost low.

options.content: Soft HRM
options.rationale: Soft HRM treats employees as assets whose commitment is developed.

options.content: Strategic HRM only
options.rationale: That is not a name for this approach.

options.content: Participative HRM only
options.rationale: That is not the term used for the cost-focused approach.

explanation: Hard HRM treats people as a resource to be managed for efficiency; soft HRM treats them as assets to be developed.

stem: What is a **zero-hours contract**?

options.content: No guaranteed hours of work
options.rationale: Correct: the employer gives work only when it is needed.

options.content: Work for a fixed number of hours every week
options.rationale: That is a standard full-time or part-time contract.

options.content: A contract for a single day of work only
options.rationale: A zero-hours contract has no fixed end date.

options.content: A contract with no pay for any hours
options.rationale: Hours worked are paid.

explanation: A zero-hours contract guarantees no minimum hours; the worker is paid only for hours actually worked.

stem: Which of the following describes **annualised hours**?

options.content: Workers choose their start and finish times each day
options.rationale: That describes flexi-time.

options.content: Two workers share one full-time job
options.rationale: That describes job sharing.

options.content: Workers are paid per task by a digital platform
options.rationale: That describes the gig economy.

options.content: A yearly total of hours set by demand
options.rationale: Correct: workers do more hours in busy periods and fewer in quiet ones.

explanation: Annualised hours spread a total of hours across the year to match demand.

stem: Which is a likely feature of **soft HRM**?

options.content: Tight control and close monitoring
options.rationale: These are features of hard HRM.

options.content: The use of workers only when cheapest
options.rationale: That is a feature of hard HRM.

options.content: Training and employee participation
options.rationale: Correct: the aim is to develop commitment.

options.content: Minimising labour costs above all else
options.rationale: That is the aim of hard HRM.

explanation: Soft HRM uses communication, training, development and participation to build motivation and loyalty.

stem: A fictional bakery in Gweru employs two cashiers who share one full-time job, one working mornings and the other afternoons. This is

options.content: Flexi-time
options.rationale: Flexi-time lets each worker choose start and finish times.

options.content: Compressed hours
options.rationale: Compressed hours put full hours into fewer days.

options.content: Job sharing
options.rationale: Correct: two people share the duties of one post.

options.content: A zero-hours contract
options.rationale: The cashiers have agreed hours.

explanation: Two workers dividing one full-time job is job sharing.
hints: How many people occupy the one post?

stem: What is the main **disadvantage for employees** of the gig economy?

options.content: Hours that are fixed every week
options.rationale: Gig work usually has no fixed hours.

options.content: Lack of security and rights
options.rationale: Correct: gig workers are self-employed and paid per task.

options.content: A guaranteed monthly salary at all times
options.rationale: Gig workers are not guaranteed a salary.

options.content: Compulsory paid holiday for all drivers
options.rationale: Self-employed workers do not normally have paid holiday.

explanation: Gig workers are paid per task, with no guaranteed work and few employment rights.
hints: Think about guaranteed hours, pay and rights.

stem: A fictional retailer in Johannesburg uses software to screen job applications. Which is the most important risk?

options.content: The software cannot process any CVs
options.rationale: Screening software processes CVs; the issue is how.

options.content: Past bias may be repeated by the selection software
options.rationale: Correct: software that learns from past decisions can copy their unfairness.

options.content: The software will refuse to be switched off
options.rationale: This is not a real risk of screening software.

options.content: Candidates can no longer apply online
options.rationale: Online application is what the software supports.

explanation: AI trained on past decisions may repeat bias, so results should be checked by people.
hints: What does the software learn from?

stem: Why might a fictional software company that needs scarce skilled programmers prefer a soft approach to HRM?

options.content: Programmers never need to be managed
options.rationale: Programmers need managing like any other staff.

options.content: Soft HRM is always the cheapest approach
options.rationale: It is often more costly in the short term.

options.content: Hard HRM is illegal for software firms
options.rationale: No such restriction exists.

options.content: Skilled staff are hard to replace
options.rationale: Correct: development and reward help to keep people who are difficult to find.

explanation: Where skills are scarce, commitment and retention matter more than low-cost flexibility.
hints: What happens if skilled staff leave?

stem: A business that uses a hard approach to HRM will normally spend more on training and employee participation than one using a soft approach.
explanation: False. A soft approach emphasises training, participation and development. A hard approach focuses on control, flexibility and cost.

stem: Match each flexible working arrangement to its description.

right.content: Two workers share one full-time job
No guaranteed hours; pay only for hours worked
Workers choose start and finish times within limits
Full hours are worked in fewer, longer days

explanation: Each is a different way of making working time flexible.

stem: Choose the correct word for each gap.

explanation: Soft HRM develops commitment; hard HRM manages people as a resource.

stem: State **one** advantage to a business of using flexible working contracts.

accepted.value: can respond to changes in demand

explanation: Accept lower labour costs, matching labour to demand, or greater flexibility in busy and quiet periods.

stem: State **one** way in which artificial intelligence can be used in human resource management.
explanation: Accept screening applications, chatbots for candidates, monitoring, training or workforce planning.

stem: A fictional safari lodge near Hwange needs 50 hours of staff time a week for 36 weeks of the year and 90 hours a week for the remaining 16 weeks. It employs two workers on annualised hours at US\$5 an hour, who are paid only for the hours needed. Calculate the annual labour cost.
explanation: Hours needed = (36 × 50) + (16 × 90) = 1,800 + 1,440 = 3,240. Cost = 3,240 × US\$5 = US\$16,200. Giving 3,240 is the number of hours, not the cost.
workedSolution: 1. Hours needed = (36 × 50) + (16 × 90) = 1,800 + 1,440 = 3,240. Cost = 3,240 × US\$5 = US\$16,200. Giving 3,240 is the number of hours, not the cost.
hints: Find the total hours needed in the year first.

stem: The lodge considers using zero-hours workers instead, paid a 15% premium on the US\$5 hourly rate but only for the 3,240 hours needed. Calculate the annual labour cost.
explanation: Hourly rate = 5 × 1.15 = US\$5.75. Cost = 3,240 × 5.75 = US\$18,630. Using the US\$5 rate gives 16,200, which ignores the premium.
workedSolution:
1. Hourly rate with premium = 5 × 1.15 = US\$5.75.
2. Annual cost = 3,240 × 5.75 = US\$18,630.
hints: Find the hourly rate with the premium first.

stem: A full-time employee works 2,080 hours a year at US\$5 an hour. If the lodge employed full-time staff to cover the peak of 90 hours a week (using the smallest whole number of staff), by how much would the annual labour cost exceed the US\$16,200 cost of annualised hours?
explanation: 90 ÷ 40 = 2.25, so 3 full-time staff are needed: 3 × 2,080 × 5 = US\$31,200. Excess over annualised hours = 31,200 − 16,200 = US\$15,000.
hints: Find how many full-time staff cover 90 hours a week, then their cost.

stem: Explain the difference between hard and soft approaches to HRM.

points.description: Hard HRM treats employees as a resource and a cost to be controlled
Soft HRM treats employees as assets whose commitment is developed
Hard uses targets, monitoring and flexible contracts; soft uses training, participation and reward

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Hard HRM treats employees as a resource and a cost to be controlled, using targets, monitoring and flexible contracts. Soft HRM treats them as assets whose commitment is developed, using training, participation and reward.

explanation: One point per mark.
hints: Compare how each views employees and the tools it uses.

stem: Analyse one advantage and one disadvantage to a fictional restaurant in Bulawayo of employing waiting staff on zero-hours contracts.

points.description: Advantage: the restaurant pays only for hours needed, so wage costs fall in quiet periods
Application: on a quiet Tuesday it need not pay staff for empty tables
Disadvantage: workers have no security and may leave for steadier jobs
Application: high turnover means the restaurant must recruit and train often, and service quality may fall

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The restaurant pays only for hours needed, so on a quiet Tuesday it does not pay staff for empty tables. But workers have no security and may leave for steadier jobs, so the restaurant must recruit and train often, and service quality may fall.

explanation: One advantage and one disadvantage, each developed.
hints: Give a cost benefit and then a staff-related cost, both applied.

stem: Assess whether a fictional bank in Lusaka should use artificial intelligence to monitor the performance of its call-centre staff.

points.description: It can measure call times and customer satisfaction accurately and cheaply
Managers can target training where it is most needed
Staff may feel watched and lose trust, which lowers morale
It may raise stress and turnover
Privacy and data rules must be followed
Judgement with a reason: use it with openness about what is measured and for support, not only control

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: AI can measure call times and customer satisfaction accurately and cheaply, and managers can target training where it is most needed. But staff may feel watched and lose trust, which lowers morale and may raise stress and turnover, and privacy and data rules must be followed. The bank should use it if it is open about what is measured and uses the results to support staff, not only to control them.

explanation: One point per mark; the judgement needs a reason or condition.
hints: Give a benefit, a risk and a condition.

stem: A fictional business: Mlambo Garden Centre in Harare needs 60 hours of staff time a week for 28 weeks of the year and 100 hours a week for 20 weeks (the spring and summer peak). The owner can employ part-timers on annualised hours at US\$4 an hour, paid only for the hours needed, or zero-hours workers at US\$4.60 an hour, paid only for the hours worked.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the total number of hours needed in the year.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate how much more the zero-hours option would cost in a year than annualised hours.
parts.explanation: Extra cost per hour = 0.60; 3,680 × 0.60 = US\$2,208. (Annualised: 14,720; zero-hours: 16,928.)
parts.workedSolution: 1. Extra cost per hour = 0.60; 3,680 × 0.60 = US\$2,208. (Annualised: 14,720; zero-hours: 16,928.)

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Evaluate which arrangement the owner should choose.

points.description: Annualised hours cost US\$2,208 less
They give workers security and may reduce turnover
Zero-hours workers cost more but may be easier to add or drop at short notice
Weather affects garden centres, so demand may differ from the plan
Judgement with a reason: annualised hours, if the demand forecast is reliable

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Annualised hours cost US\$2,208 less and give workers security, which may reduce turnover and keep experienced staff. Zero-hours workers cost more but can be added or dropped at short notice, which helps if the weather changes demand. If the forecast of demand is reliable, annualised hours are the better choice.

parts.explanation: Cost and flexibility weighed with a condition.

explanation: 3,680 hours; zero hours cost US\$2,208 more; annualised hours are better if the forecast holds.
hints: Hours needed = weeks × hours per week for each period, added together.

stem: A fictional business: Khumalo Couriers of Bulawayo delivers parcels using 40 self-employed drivers paid per delivery through a mobile phone app. The app tracks each driver's speed and ranks drivers by customer ratings. Drivers with low ratings receive fewer jobs. The company's costs are low, but turnover among drivers is 60% a year and the owner has received complaints about late deliveries.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Khumalo Couriers' use of self-employed drivers paid per delivery is an example of

options.content: Job sharing
options.rationale: No drivers share a post.

options.content: Flexi-time
options.rationale: Drivers do not choose hours within an employer's pattern.

options.content: Annualised hours
options.rationale: Hours are not scheduled over a year.

options.content: The gig economy
options.rationale: Correct: self-employed workers paid per task through a digital platform.

parts.explanation: Payment per task through a platform is the gig economy.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Analyse two ways in which the app's monitoring might affect the drivers.

points.description: Constant tracking may make drivers feel watched and under pressure
Application: drivers may hurry, increasing accidents and late deliveries
Ranking by customer ratings may lead drivers to fear loss of work
Application: drivers with low ratings receive fewer jobs, so they may leave for another platform

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Constant tracking of speed may make drivers feel watched and under pressure, so they may hurry, which can increase accidents and late deliveries. Ranking by ratings makes them fear loss of work, and drivers who receive fewer jobs may leave for another platform.

hints: Link monitoring to feelings, then behaviour.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Evaluate whether Khumalo Couriers should change from a hard approach to a softer approach to managing its drivers.

points.description: The hard approach keeps costs low and allows quick changes in the number of drivers
Turnover of 60% and complaints about late deliveries show costs: recruitment, training and lost customers
A softer approach might include training, minimum earnings, feedback and a say in the app's rules
Soft changes cost money and reduce flexibility
The right approach depends on how much the company's reputation for reliable delivery matters
Judgement with a reason and condition, for example move part-way to a softer approach for the best drivers

levels.descriptor: Weighs low cost and flexibility against turnover and reliability using the case; considers a softer package; a justified recommendation with a condition
Explains the two approaches with some use of the case; judgement weakly supported
Describes hard and soft HRM with little application

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The hard approach keeps costs low and lets the company change the number of drivers quickly. But turnover of 60% and complaints about late deliveries show the costs: constant recruitment and training and lost customers. A softer approach, with training, a minimum earnings guarantee, feedback and a say in the app's rules, might keep the best drivers and improve reliability, although it would cost money and reduce flexibility. The right approach depends on how much the company's reputation for reliable delivery matters. Khumalo Couriers should move part-way to a softer approach for its best drivers and keep flexibility for the rest, then review turnover and complaints after six months.

parts.explanation: Weighs flexibility and cost against turnover and reliability and recommends a partial change.
hints: Compare the cost savings with the costs shown by turnover and complaints.

explanation: Gig economy; monitoring causes pressure and leaving; a partial move to a softer approach may fit the company's reliability goal.
hints: Link the app's rules to drivers' behaviour.

stem: A fictional business: Mutendi Financial Services of Harare has 200 staff and receives 5,000 job applications a year. HR managers spend about 1,500 hours a year reading applications. A software supplier offers an AI system that screens CVs and ranks applicants, at a cost of US\$18,000 a year, and could reduce the HR time spent to 300 hours. HR time costs the company US\$15 an hour.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the annual saving in HR time if the system is introduced, before deducting the cost of the system.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Analyse one benefit and one risk of the AI system for the company.

points.description: Benefit: faster shortlisting, saving HR time
Application: 1,200 fewer hours spent reading applications
Risk: the system may repeat past bias or reject good candidates with unusual CVs
Application: the company could miss talented applicants and face complaints of unfairness

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The system would shortlist faster and save 1,200 hours of HR time. But it might repeat past bias or reject good candidates with unusual CVs, so the company could miss talented applicants and face complaints of unfairness.

parts.explanation: A benefit and a risk, each applied.
hints: Use the figures in the case.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Evaluate whether Mutendi Financial Services should introduce the AI system.

points.description: The direct saving equals the cost of the system (US\$18,000), so there is no net financial gain
Benefits not in the saving: faster responses to candidates, and HR staff free for other work
Risks: bias, unfairness, loss of personal contact, and applicants' data
The company can check a sample of rejected applications to reduce the risk
Soft HRM suggests that human contact with candidates builds the company's reputation
Judgement with a reason and time-frame, for example a trial for a year with human checks

levels.descriptor: Uses the cost and saving figures and the risks from the case; considers safeguards and non-financial factors; a justified recommendation with a time-frame
Explains benefits and risks with some use of the figures; judgement weakly supported
Describes AI in recruitment with little application

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The saving in HR time is worth US\$18,000, exactly the cost of the system, so there is no net financial gain in the first year. The benefits that remain are faster responses to candidates and HR staff freed for other work, but the risks are that the system repeats bias, rejects good applicants and removes personal contact, and it holds personal data. The company can check a sample of rejected applications to reduce the risk. Because the financial case is neutral and the risks are real, Mutendi should run a one-year trial with human checks and decide on continuing after reviewing the quality of appointments.

parts.explanation: Weighs a neutral financial case against benefits and risks and recommends a trial.
hints: Compare the saving with the cost, then weigh the other benefits and risks.

explanation: Saving US\$18,000 equals the cost; the case rests on non-financial benefits and risks; trial with human checks.
hints: Hours saved × hourly cost of HR time.
